title: Parmanand: hear, then do
hookLine: what use is hearing holy stories if devotion doesn't follow (Sarang, Parmanand, ang 1253)

cards: A cookbook on the nightstand, its pages soft from reading in bed. Every recipe known by heart. The oven has never been switched on.
Reading about bread is a real pleasure. It just doesn't feed anybody.
In Raag Sarang, on Ang 1253 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Bhagat Parmanand turns to someone who has heard every holy story there is, and asks a blunt question: so what did all that listening do?

teach.h: WHAT DID HEARING THE PURANAS GAIN YOU?
teach.b: Parmanand is one of the Bhagats, the devotees outside the line of the Gurus whose words sit in the Granth. The Granth tells almost nothing about his life; what it keeps is his hymn.
It opens, in paraphrase: man, what have you gained by hearing the Puranas? Steady devotion never rose up in you, and you gave nothing to the hungry.
The Puranas are old books of sacred stories, gods and kings and devotees, read aloud and loved. Parmanand isn't sneering at the stories.

teach.h: NOT THE STORIES: THE UNCHANGED LISTENER.
teach.b: He's looking at the listener who walks away from them unchanged. Then he names what didn't move: lust and anger and greed are still there, and the mouth still hasn't stopped speaking ill of others.
The stories went in at the ears and stopped. Look at his test. Not how many stories you know, or how beautifully you retell them.

teach.h: TWO TESTS: DEVOTION, AND THE HUNGRY FED.
teach.b: Two plain questions: did devotion grow, and did the hungry get fed? A heart turned toward God, and a hand turned toward the person in front of you, named side by side, and the listener has neither.
The Granth keeps that question in his own voice. Which is a little awkward for a lesson like this one, since a lesson is also something heard.
A story heard is a seed in a pocket.
Parmanand's question is whether it ever goes into the ground.

how: Parmanand's hymn in Raag Sarang is sung in kirtan like other Gurbani, and Sikhs read it as a call to let what is heard in the gurdwara change how they live and give.

o: a storyteller who recited the Puranas at court
the Bhagat who asked what hearing holy stories gained
a Guru who wrote the Granth's longest hymn

games.q: inside the hymn — tap the pairs.
p: went in at the ears and stopped

s: he questions the listener who hears them and walks away unchanged.
the hymn tests devotion and feeding the hungry together
steady devotion didn't rise, and the hungry got nothing: both count against the listener.
the Granth tells us a lot about Parmanand's life
it keeps his name and his hymn, and little else.

games.q: you've heard holy stories for years and can retell them all. what does Parmanand ask you?
o: how many more stories do you know?
what did all that hearing change?
why do you bother listening at all?
games.why: he asks what was gained: did devotion grow, did the hungry get fed? the hearing isn't the problem; staying unchanged is.

practice: Bring back one story from this path lately: Sain offering his work, Pipa finding the temple in the body, Ramanand at home in a house colored with love.

Hold it, and ask what it would look like as one small thing done, a meal shared, a sharp word left unsaid, until it feels like a plan instead of a wish. If you pray, Waheguru can go with each breath out.

wordCard.voice: Parmanand. A Bhagat whose hymn in Raag Sarang asks what the hearing was for, if devotion never grew and the hungry went unfed.

carryVoice: Your line: hear, then do. Listening is the start, not the finish. Day seven hundred eighty-seven.
